insider_note: The whole answer turns on one enzyme having two jobs. Say RuBisCO binds BOTH carbon dioxide and oxygen in the first two lines and the rest follows.

steps.label: RuBisCO and its two substrates
steps.margin_note: Name the enzyme in full and say it takes both gases. The affinity line matters.
lines: RuBisCO is the most abundant enzyme in the
world.
Its active site can bind BOTH carbon dioxide
and oxygen. That is why it is named
ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase-oxygenase.
It has a much greater affinity for CO2 than
for O2.
steps.why: One active site that accepts two different gases is the whole cause of photorespiration, so the enzyme's double name is the first thing to write.
common_mistakes: Saying RuBisCO binds only carbon dioxide. It binds oxygen too, and that is the point.
Saying it prefers oxygen. It has a much GREATER affinity for carbon dioxide.
steps.memory_tip: Carboxylase and oxygenase in one name: two jobs, one active site.

steps.label: What happens when oxygen wins
steps.margin_note: Give the normal equation first so the departure from it is visible.
lines: Normally CO2 binds and the Calvin cycle runs:
But if the oxygen concentration is HIGH,
RuBisCO acts as an OXYGENASE and binds O2
instead.
This pathway is called PHOTORESPIRATION.
steps.why: Which gas binds depends on which is more plentiful, so photorespiration is not a separate mechanism but the same enzyme meeting a different gas.
common_mistakes: Saying photorespiration is a separate enzyme's work. It is the SAME enzyme, RuBisCO.
Leaving out the condition. It happens when the OXYGEN concentration is high.
steps.memory_tip: Same enzyme, different gas, different pathway.

steps.label: The products
steps.margin_note: Name both products and say which one is useless.
lines: Instead of two molecules of PGA, the reaction
gives only ONE:
one molecule of phosphoglycerate and
one molecule of PHOSPHOGLYCOLATE.
Phosphoglycolate is a 2-carbon compound and is
of no use to the Calvin cycle.
steps.why: Half the usual product is lost to a two-carbon compound the cycle cannot use, which is the measurable cost of photorespiration.
common_mistakes: Saying two PGA are still formed. Only ONE PGA is formed, plus phosphoglycolate.
Calling phosphoglycolate a 3-carbon compound. It has TWO carbons.
steps.memory_tip: Two products, only one of them useful.

steps.label: Why it is wasteful
steps.margin_note: Three negatives and one release. This is the mark for the word 'wasteful'.

lines.text: No sugar, no ATP, no NADPH — and CO2 lost

lines: In photorespiration there is NO synthesis of
sugar, NO synthesis of ATP and NO synthesis of
NADPH.
Carbon dioxide is RELEASED and ATP is USED UP.
Photorespiration is therefore a wasteful
process.
steps.why: A pathway that consumes ATP, releases carbon dioxide and makes nothing is a net loss on every count, which is what the word wasteful is being asked to justify.
common_mistakes: Saying photorespiration makes a little ATP. It makes NONE and consumes ATP.
Saying carbon dioxide is fixed. It is RELEASED.
steps.memory_tip: It spends ATP and gives back carbon dioxide: a loss on both sides.
